text: Everything so far in this course has been a hand-built comparison, lesson by lesson, so you could see exactly what changes between dialects and why. A real migration -- moving a production application off SQL Server and onto Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, or a cloud warehouse -- is too large to translate line by line. Real teams lean on the vendor's own migration guide, and usually an automated tool that reads that guide's rules and applies them at scale. Your job isn't to memorize every rule. It's to know what to look for, so you can sanity-check the tool's output and finish what it can't.

Every real migration guide -- Oracle's, AWS's, Microsoft's, it doesn't matter which -- organizes itself around the same three concerns, and they get harder to resolve automatically as you go down the list. First, data type mapping tables: a row-by-row lookup from a source type to its nearest target equivalent, built from exactly the comparisons Chapter 2 of this course covered. Second, a list of unsupported or differently-behaving functions -- this is where you'll find entries like ISNULL versus NVL versus IFNULL versus COALESCE, laid out for lookup. And third, procedural code: stored procedures, functions, triggers, packages. That third section is almost always flagged as needing the most manual rework, because procedural dialects diverge the most of anything this course has shown you.

These tools are not hypothetical -- they're what real companies actually run migrations on. Oracle SQL Developer has a built-in Migration Workbench, under Tools, Migration, that connects to a source database, commonly SQL Server, captures its schema, and generates equivalent Oracle objects plus a first pass at translating simpler procedural code into PL/SQL. AWS Schema Conversion Tool, SCT, connects a source engine to a target -- commonly Aurora MySQL, Aurora PostgreSQL, or Redshift -- and produces an assessment report: what percentage converted automatically, and an explicit list of action items for anything it couldn't handle alone. And Azure Database Migration Service, usually paired with the free Data Migration Assistant for the compatibility check, migrates SQL Server workloads into Azure SQL, flagging blocking issues before the migration actually runs.

Here's what a real mapping table entry looks like, and notice it's the exact same comparison you already know how to make from Chapter 2 -- just laid out for lookup instead of narration. DATETIME2 maps to TIMESTAMP on Oracle, but the note says check the fractional-seconds scale, because precision doesn't always map one to one. NVARCHAR of n maps to NVARCHAR2 of n, but Oracle's max length depends on the database's character set. BIT maps to NUMBER of 1, because Oracle has no native boolean type at all -- which Lesson 9 already told you directly. When you open a real mapping table for the first time, read it exactly this way: find the type you already understand, then check the note column for the one detail keeping it from being a clean swap.

Every guide eventually arrives at a section called something like Converting Stored Procedures, and every single one of them says some version of the same thing: automated tools translate basic query syntax well, but procedural objects almost always need a human to finish the job. AWS SCT's own assessment reports literally count this, as action items, per object. That's not a failure of the tooling -- it's a direct consequence of everything Chapters 5 through 8 already showed you. TRY CATCH has no literal MySQL equivalent. PL/SQL packages have no T-SQL equivalent at all. And cursors behave differently enough across all four platforms that no tool can safely guess your intent every time.

To recap: every real migration guide covers data type mapping, function differences, and procedural code, roughly in that order of increasing manual effort -- and Oracle's Migration Workbench, AWS's Schema Conversion Tool, and Azure's Database Migration Service are the genuine tools built around exactly that structure. Next lesson, we pull together the recurring pitfalls this entire course has surfaced into one practical checklist you can run before anything ships to production. See you there.
